transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello doctor. I suppose... well, my family thought I should come in, and I guess they’re right, because I just don’t have the push I used to have. It’s hard to explain. I used to be so busy, you know? Always doing something, always on the move. I was in the church choir for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, singing every Sunday morning. And then there was my quilting group. We meet—well, they meet—over at the community center on Wednesdays. We were working on this beautiful star pattern, all these tiny little pieces you have to stitch together just right, and I was always the one organizing the fabric. And I used to love visiting folks, too, taking a pie over if someone was under the weather or just sitting on the porch to chat the afternoon away. 

But lately... I just don't have it in me. I don't have that drive at all. Most days, I don't even leave the house. I just sit there in my recliner in the living room with the TV on. I keep the volume down real low, so it's just sort of flickering in the background, not really watching it, just staring at the screen. And the terrible thing is, I know people are expecting me. The choir director called twice last week, and I know the quilting ladies are wondering where I am and waiting on me to finish my squares, but I just... I just sit there in the quiet. I can't seem to make myself get up and go out the door anymore, no matter how much I know I ought to. I just sit there.
Do you still enjoy the things you used to do, like singing in the choir or quilting?

Enjoy them? Well... I don't rightly know if it's about enjoying them anymore, because like I was just saying, I just don’t have the push for any of it. I don't know if I'd enjoy it if I actually got there, because I can't even get myself out the door to find out. 

I think about the choir, and Reverend Thomas picking out the hymns—he always picks the good old ones, you know—and I know I used to feel a real warmth in my heart singing them. But now, I just sit there in my chair. I look over at my sewing basket sitting by the coffee table with all those little blue and yellow squares for the quilting group, and I know they're expecting me, I really do. I know they need my pieces to finish the border. But I just don't feel that spark to pick up the needle. I don't feel much of anything about it, to be honest. 

So I just stay right there at home, most days. Just me and the recliner, with that TV on low. Just watching the pictures move across the screen without even listening to what the people on the shows are saying. It's like the part of me that used to love visiting folks and doing all those busy things just... went to sleep, I guess. I sit there and I think, "I should go, they're waiting on me," but the feeling of actually wanting to do it, the fun of it... it's just washed right out of me.
Do you feel pleasure in anything at all anymore?

Pleasure? Oh, doctor, I... I don't think so. I really don't. It all comes back to what I was telling you before, about how I just don't have that push anymore. The push for the choir, the push for the quilting, the push for going over to see Mrs. Higgins when her arthritis flares up... it's all just gone. And if you don't have the push to do a thing, how can you find pleasure in it? 

I used to find pleasure in so many things. Just the smell of a fresh pie coming out of the oven, or the way the harmony sounded when the sopranos and altos finally got that tricky part in 'How Great Thou Art' just perfect. But now... now it's just me and that recliner. Most days, that's all it is. I just sit there at home, right in the living room, with the TV turned down so low you can barely hear a whisper from it. And I sit there knowing—I know it in my head, plain as day—that people are expecting me. I know the ladies need my blue and yellow squares for the border of that star quilt, and I know Reverend Thomas is looking out at the choir loft wondering where my voice went. But knowing they're expecting me doesn't bring any pleasure, and it doesn't bring any push to get up and go. It just feels like... like everything is just flat. Just sitting there, watching the pictures move on the screen, feeling nothing at all about it.
Do you ever think about death or wish you weren't alive?

Death? Oh, Lord, no. No, doctor, it’s nothing like that. I don't sit there wishing I'd pass on or anything of the sort. It's not a sadness like that, where you just want to cry and leave the world behind. I don't want to die. I just... well, like I keep saying, I just don't have the push to do the living part the way I used to. 

I don't sit in my recliner thinking about the end, or wishing the good Lord would come take me. My aunt Mary, now, she used to talk like that when her hips got so bad she couldn't even walk down to the mailbox, always saying she was just ready to go home to Jesus and be done with it all. But I don't feel like that at all. I don't have any aches or pains making me miserable like she did, and I don't have any dark thoughts about harming myself. I wouldn't ever do a thing like that. 

It's just... it's just that flatness I was telling you about. Like the TV being on but the sound being turned all the way down to a whisper. I'm just sitting there in the room. I know the day is passing, I see the sun come through the front window and move across the rug, and I know I ought to be over at the community center with the ladies finishing those star squares, but I just watch the light move instead. I don't wish I wasn't alive. I just don't feel much like doing anything with the life I've got right now, if that makes any sense to you. I just let the hours roll right on by me. So no, I don't think about death at all. I'm just sitting.
How long have you been feeling this way, without the push to do things?

How long? Well... let me think back on it now. It hasn't been a sudden thing, doctor, not like waking up one morning with a bad cold. It’s been building... yes, it's been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now. 

I used to work down there, you see, answering the phones and sorting the mail for the teachers, making sure the little ones who scraped their knees on the playground got a wet paper towel while they waited for the nurse. I was always busy, always on my feet, always having somewhere I needed to be. And then, a little over two years ago, I retired. They gave me a nice little party in the breakroom, a big sheet cake with pink frosting, and everybody kept telling me I was going to have so much time for my quilting and my choir now. And I really believed I would. I brought home the nice little clock they gave me, set it right there on the mantel, and I thought to myself that I could finally just catch my breath. 

So I sat down in my recliner. I figured I was just resting, you know? Just taking a well-deserved break after all those years of the morning bell and the afternoon buses. But the rest just... it just kept stretching out. The weeks turned into months, and that push to get back up and do things, it just never came back to me. It's like a slow leak in a bicycle tire. You don't notice it all at once, but the air just keeps seeping out, bit by bit, day by day, until you look down and the whole thing is just completely flat against the pavement. That's exactly how it's been since I left that office two years ago. Just two years of the push leaking right out of me, getting flatter and flatter, until now I just sit there with the TV turned down to a whisper, letting the daylight move across the rug.
Do you feel tired all the time?

Tired? Well... no, doctor, I wouldn't call it tired. It's not like that heavy feeling you get in your bones after you've spent the whole day scrubbing the kitchen floor on your hands and knees, or when you've been up half the night canning tomatoes because they all ripened on the vine at the exact same time. It's not a physical tiredness, if you see what I mean. 

I'm not sleepy. I sleep fine at night, usually. I just sit in that recliner all day, so I haven't done anything to make my body tired. It's more just... well, like I was saying, it's the push that's missing, not the energy. If the house caught fire, I suppose I'd have the energy to get up and walk out the door, but short of that... I just don't feel the need to move. It's not exhaustion. My arms and legs don't ache with weariness. I just don't have the will to make them do anything. I just sit there and let the time pass. So no, I wouldn't say I'm tired. I'm just... still. Just very, very still.
Have you experienced a significant loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed over the past two years?

Well, yes, doctor, that’s exactly it. That’s really the whole reason what brings me in here today, to be honest with you. It’s the choir, and the quilting, and just... visiting folks. I used to love all of that. I sang alto down at the church for near on thirty years, never missed a Wednesday night practice unless the snow was too high to drive in. I loved getting up there and singing the old hymns, feeling like I was a part of something big and beautiful. And the quilting... I was telling you about those star squares earlier. We were making a beautiful double wedding ring pattern for the pastor's niece, and I was always the fastest stitcher in the group. I used to love going over to the community center, drinking weak coffee out of those little styrofoam cups and catching up with the ladies. I used to bake a pecan pie and just go visiting folks, checking in on my neighbors, making sure everybody was doing alright. 

But over these past two years... I just don’t have the push I used to have for any of it. I don't have the push for choir, I don't have the push for quilting, and I sure don't have the push to go visiting folks. The want-to is just gone. 

Most days... well, most days I just sit at home in my recliner. I keep the TV on low, just murmuring in the background like I told you, and I just sit. And the thing of it is, doctor, I know people are expecting me. I know they are. I know the choir director is looking at my empty seat in the second row, and I know the ladies at the center are wondering who's going to finish my corner of that quilt, and I know my neighbor is wondering why I haven't come knocking on her screen door in a month of Sundays. I know they're all expecting me to walk through the door. I know it in my head. But I just sit there with the TV on low, watching the daylight move across the floor, and I just can't bring myself to get up and go do the things I used to love. The interest... the push... it just isn't there anymore.
Have you experienced any changes in your appetite over the past two years?

My appetite? Well... no, doctor, I wouldn't say there's been any real change there. Not that I can think of. I mean, I still eat, of course. I have to eat. It's just... well, it's like everything else, isn't it? The push just isn't there to make a big fuss about it. 

I used to love cooking, you know. I used to make these big Sunday dinners—pot roast with carrots and potatoes, the kind that cooks low and slow all afternoon so the whole house smells like gravy and rosemary by the time three o'clock rolls around. I'd make yeast rolls from scratch, kneading the dough right there on the floury counter, letting it rise in the warm spot by the stove. I loved doing that. But now... well, now it's just me, and since I'm just sitting in that recliner most of the day, I don't work up a big hunger. 

I still eat my meals, though. I'll get up and maybe heat up a can of soup—chicken noodle or tomato, usually—or I'll make a piece of toast with a little butter and maybe a scrape of marmalade if I'm feeling up to opening the jar. Sometimes I'll just have a bowl of cornflakes in the evening while the TV is murmuring. But I eat. I don't feel like I'm starving, and I haven't noticed my clothes hanging off me or anything like that. My skirts still fit the same around the waist. It's just that the food is... it's just fuel now, I suppose. It's not an event. I just eat what's easy, what doesn't take any effort to put together, because standing at the stove stirring a pot just feels like a mountain I don't need to climb. So my appetite itself is fine, I suppose, just... simple. Very simple.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving or speaking more slowly? Well... no, doctor, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that, and nobody's said anything to me about it. I mean, I'm sixty-seven years old, so I'm not exactly running footraces down the street like I did when I was a girl in pigtails, but I don't feel like I'm moving through molasses or anything. 

When I do get up out of the recliner, like to go to the kitchen to heat up that soup I was telling you about, or to use the restroom, my legs work just fine. I walk at a normal pace, I suppose. It's not like my joints are rusted shut. It's just that I don't get up very often, like I said. The sitting still isn't because I can't move fast, it's just because I don't have the push to move at all. But when I do move, it's just regular moving. 

And as for speaking... well, you're listening to me right now, aren't you? I don't think I'm talking any slower than I ever did. I've always been a talker, doctor. My late husband, God rest his soul, used to say I could talk the ears off a brass monkey. He'd sit there at the kitchen table reading the evening paper, and I'd be at the sink washing up the supper dishes, just chattering away about the neighbor's dog or what the price of butter was down at the market, and he'd just nod and turn the page. I've always had plenty to say, and I don't feel like the words are getting stuck in my throat or taking a long time to come out. They just tumble out same as they always did. 

So no, I wouldn't say I'm moving slow or talking slow. I just... I just don't have anywhere I need to be in a hurry, so I just stay put. But the speed of it all... no, that hasn't changed.
Have you experienced any feelings of worthlessness or guilt over the past two years?

Worthlessness? Guilt? Well... no, doctor. No, I can't say that I have. I mean, I know I was just telling you about how I sit in my chair all day and how I know folks are expecting me down at the church and the community center, and I suppose a person could feel guilty about that. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she feels guilty if she forgets to water her petunias for a single afternoon. She'll go on and on about it over the fence. But me... I don't feel guilty, exactly. It's more like... well, it's just the way things are right now. I don't have the push to go, so I don't go. I don't sit there beating my chest and crying over it or thinking I've committed some terrible sin just because my seat in the alto section is empty. 

And as for feeling worthless... oh, heavens no. I wouldn't ever use a word like that about myself. I might not have a fancy education—I had to leave school back in the eighth grade to help my mother with the house, you know—but I've always known my value. I've worked hard my whole life. I kept a clean home, made sure my late husband always had a hot supper waiting for him, and I've been a good friend to the people in my neighborhood for decades. Just because I've lost the want-to for my quilting and my visiting doesn't mean I think I'm a piece of trash thrown out on the curb. I know I'm a good person. I'm just a good person who sits in a recliner with the TV murmuring all day. 

You know, Pastor Miller down at the church, he used to preach a lot about guilt. He'd get up there on a Sunday morning, sweating right through his good suit, talking about how guilt is a heavy winter coat you don't need to be wearing in the summertime. And I always took that to heart. I haven't done anything wrong, doctor. I haven't stolen anything or spoken ill of anybody or hurt a fly. I'm just... staying put, I suppose you could say. So no, I don't feel worthless, and I don't feel guilty. I just feel exactly like I told you before—like the push has just up and left me, and I don't have the energy to feel bad about it.
Do you feel sad most of the day?

Sad? Well... no, doctor. I wouldn't say I feel sad. People always seem to think that if you're sitting alone in a house all day, not doing much of anything, you must be just weeping into a handkerchief from dawn to dusk, but that's not how it is for me at all. 

When my husband passed—God rest him—now, that was sad. I remember sitting at our kitchen table, the one with the yellow formica top that we bought over at Sears back in the seventies, and I'd just cry until my ribs ached and my eyes were completely puffed shut. I couldn't even look at his old work boots by the back door without bursting into tears. That's what sadness feels like to me. It's sharp, and it's heavy, and it hurts right in the middle of your chest. 

But what I have now... it doesn't hurt. It doesn't feel like much of anything at all, really. I just sit in my recliner, like I told you, and the TV is going—maybe "The Price is Right" or one of those old black-and-white westerns he used to like—and I just watch the colors on the screen. I don't feel like crying. I don't feel blue or down in the dumps. 

My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she gets the blues sometimes, especially in the winter when the days get short and the sun goes down by four o'clock, and she'll lean over the fence and sigh and talk about how dreary everything is. But I don't feel dreary. I just feel... blank, I suppose. Like a chalkboard that nobody's written on today. I'm not happy, I'm not jumping for joy or smiling at the birds out the window, but I'm certainly not sad. I think it actually takes a lot of energy to drum up a big emotion like sadness. It takes a lot out of a person to be sad, to cry and fret, don't you think? And I just don't have that kind of push in me anymore. So no, no sadness. Just... quiet.
Do you still take pleasure in the simple things, like eating your favorite foods or taking a warm bath?

Pleasure? Oh, I don't know about pleasure, doctor. I mean, take food, for instance. I used to make a pot roast every Sunday... carrots, onions, potatoes, the whole nine yards. My late husband loved it, and I'd look forward to that meal all week long. Now? I just heat up whatever's in the pantry, like that canned chicken noodle soup I mentioned before, and it's just... well, it's just fuel, I suppose. It doesn't taste bad, but it doesn't make me close my eyes and smile like it used to. It's just something to put in my stomach so it stops rumbling. 

And a warm bath... well, we have a nice deep tub that was put in back in the nineties, and I used to soak in there with lavender Epsom salts for an hour on a Tuesday evening. It was my little luxury. But now, getting the water running, getting in, getting out and getting dried off... it just feels like a list of steps I have to take to get clean, not anything I'd call a treat. I'd almost rather just use a washcloth at the sink and be done with it. 

And really, I suppose that's the whole crux of it. That's exactly what brings me in here to see you. I just don't have the push I used to have for... well, for anything. Not for my choir, not for my quilting circle, not even for visiting folks around the neighborhood. I used to be the first one at the church doors on Sunday morning, ready to sing, and I always had a quilt square in my lap if I was sitting down. Now, most days I just sit at home in my recliner with the TV on low. I don't even have the volume turned up loud enough to really hear the words half the time, just the murmur of the commercials. And I know people are expecting me—like I said, Mrs. Gable probably looks over the fence wondering where I am, and Pastor Miller surely notices my empty seat—but I just stay put. The joy of doing those things, the pleasure of it... it's just gone flat. So no, I wouldn't say I'm taking much pleasure in the simple things, or the big things either, for that matter. I just sit there with the TV on.
Do you find it difficult to initiate or complete tasks, even simple ones like getting dressed in the morning?

Getting dressed in the morning? Well... yes, I suppose that falls right in line with everything else we've been talking about, doctor. It's funny you mention getting dressed, because I was just looking at my closet the other day—it's a nice big cedar-lined closet my late husband built for us back in '82—and I was looking at all my nice blouses. I have this lovely peach-colored one with the pearl buttons that I always used to wear to Sunday service, and a navy blue skirt that matches it perfectly. I used to get up at six-thirty sharp, wash my face, set my hair, and put on a proper outfit every single morning, even if I was just going to be sweeping the front porch or walking down to the corner store for milk. My mother always taught me you never know who you're going to run into, so you ought to look presentable. 

But lately... well, getting those clothes off the hangers just feels like trying to lift a fifty-pound sack of flour. I wake up, and I sit on the edge of the mattress, and I think about the buttons, and the zippers, and finding the matching shoes, and I just... I can't seem to make my hands do it. It's too many steps. So I just stay in my flannel nightgown. Sometimes I'll put my pink chenille robe over it if the hallway is drafty, and I'll slide into my slippers, but that's about as far as I get with getting dressed. 

And really, doctor, like I've been trying to explain to you, that's the whole reason I'm here. What brings me in is I just don't have the push I used to have for my choir, or my quilting, or visiting folks around the neighborhood. And if I don't have the push to do those things, why would I have the push to put on my peach blouse and do up all those tiny pearl buttons? I know people are expecting me—Pastor Miller, Mrs. Gable, the ladies in the alto section—they're all probably wondering why I'm not out and about in my regular clothes. But instead of getting dressed and going out, most days I just sit at home in that recliner with the TV on low. I don't even bother turning it up, just let it murmur while I sit there in my nightgown. It's just so terribly hard to get started on anything at all when that want-to has completely up and left you.
Do you find it difficult to make decisions, even about small, everyday things?

Decisions? Well, no, doctor, I can't say that I do. I don't have any trouble making decisions, mostly because... well, there really aren't many decisions left to make, to be perfectly honest with you. 

Now, back when my husband was alive, we had to make all sorts of decisions. Like when we bought that yellow formica table from Sears that I told you about, we stood in that showroom for a good hour trying to decide between the yellow and a sort of mint green color they had. He liked the green, but I thought the yellow would brighten up the kitchen since our window faces north and doesn't get that good morning light. And with my quilting, oh my, I used to spend just ages at the fabric store trying to decide between a pink gingham or a blue calico for the border of a baby quilt. I'd hem and haw and hold the bolts of fabric up to the light. 

But nowadays? The choices I have to make are so small, and I just don't care enough to fret over them. Take my lunch, for instance. I'll shuffle into the kitchen in my slippers, and I'll open the pantry door, and maybe I see that canned chicken noodle soup I mentioned, and right next to it is a can of tomato soup that Mrs. Gable brought over a few weeks back when they had a buy-one-get-one sale at the Piggly Wiggly. I don't stand there wringing my hands, wondering which one would taste better or what I'm in the mood for, because I'm not in the mood for anything. I just reach my hand out, grab whatever my fingers touch first, and that's what I heat up. 

It's the exact same thing with the television. I have the remote control sitting right there on the armrest of my recliner—it's one of those universal remotes with the big buttons because my eyes aren't quite what they used to be—and I don't sit there flipping through the channels trying to decide what's best to watch. I just press the red power button, and whatever channel it was left on yesterday is what I watch today. If it's a game show, or a local news broadcast, or a half-hour commercial for a blender, it doesn't make a lick of difference to me. I just let it play. 

So it's not that my mind is muddy, or that I can't make a choice. If you asked me to pick between two things right now, I'd just point to one and be done with it. It's just that one thing is exactly the same as the other to me now. There's no right or wrong choice when you're just sitting in your nightgown all day watching the colors flash on the screen. So no, doctor, no trouble making decisions. I just don't have much of anything important left to decide on.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or restless, or do you feel like you're moving in slow motion compared to how you used to?

Slow motion... well, mostly I'm just sitting still in that recliner, like I told you. But restless? Fidgety? Now that... that is a funny thing you bring up, doctor. 

Because just the other week, Mrs. Gable—bless her heart, she just wouldn't take no for an answer, leaning right over the fence—she finally badgered me into going down to the senior center on Elm Street with her. They have this big room in the basement there where everybody gathers, and they have all these heavy metal folding chairs, the tan ones that squeak real loud when you open them up. 

Well, I was sitting there, and I wasn't really talking to anybody, just sort of staring at the floorboards, and suddenly I just got up. I started grabbing those heavy metal chairs and dragging them all across the linoleum. I was lining them all up, one right behind the other, facing the front wall just exactly like we used to have them set up back in the third grade at the old county schoolhouse. Just rows and rows, making little aisles between them. 

And then later on, when the ladies were trying to get a quilting circle going at one of the tables—they had all these little squares laid out, hoping I'd join in since they know I used to love it—I picked up this one square. It was a yellow calico piece. But I didn't start sewing. I just started folding it. I folded it in half, and then in quarters, and then I'd unfold it, smooth it out flat on my knee, and then I'd fold it all over again. Just over and over and over. 

Mary Lou and the other ladies, they kept looking at each other, and finally they started saying, "Honey, what are you doing to that fabric? You're going to wear out the edges, please stop." But I just couldn't seem to quit. I just kept right on folding and creasing it. 

And the strangest part of the whole afternoon, doctor... when they finally got me to set that yellow square down, and they asked me why I was moving all those chairs around earlier and messing with the fabric like that... I couldn't tell them. I couldn't rightly explain what I was doing or why I was doing it. My mind was just a complete blank on the matter. It wasn't like I was trying to be helpful with the chairs, or trying to make a special pattern with the quilt... my hands were just doing it all on their own. So I suppose that's a kind of restlessness, just not the normal foot-tapping kind of fidgeting most folks do.
Do you feel like you're moving at a slower pace than you used to, or do you find yourself doing things more quickly than before?

Slower or faster? Well... no, I wouldn't say my actual speed of doing things has changed one way or the other. It's funny you ask that, because just yesterday, the mail carrier—that's Mr. Henderson, he's been walking our route for going on fifteen years now, ever since his oldest boy went off to the community college over in the next county—he dropped a package on the front porch. 

I heard a big loud thump. Now, I was sitting right there in my recliner in my nightgown, just like I was telling you, and I had the television on. It was some program about... oh, I think they were restoring old farm tractors, not that I care a lick about tractors, but the bright green and red paint looked nice flashing on the screen. Anyway, I heard that thump, and I got up to go look out the front screen door to see what he'd left. 

And you know, I didn't feel like I was walking through molasses, but I certainly wasn't rushing like a house on fire, either. I just walked my regular walk. Straight down the hallway, past that old grandfather clock my husband bought at an estate sale back in '95—it doesn't even chime anymore because I haven't had the man out to fix the weights in I don't know how long. I just shuffled along at the exact same pace I've always walked. 

So my legs and my arms, they move at their usual speed, doctor. It's just getting the notion to use them that's the hard part, like I said about getting dressed. But once I'm actually up and moving across the room? No, I haven't noticed being fast or slow. Just my regular old self, really.
Do you think you would be able to regain your motivation if something or someone encouraged you?

Encouraged me? Well... see, that's the thing of it, doctor. It's not for a lack of folks trying. Just last week, Pastor Miller from the church, he called on the telephone, let it ring and ring until the answering machine finally picked up. And Mrs. Gable, she's always hollering over the fence or knocking on the screen door. 

But... well, to be honest with you, that's really the whole reason I'm here talking to you today. What brings me in is I just don't have the push I used to have. I used to have so much get-up-and-go, you wouldn't believe it. I was in the church choir for twenty-two years, singing alto, wearing those heavy maroon robes that just bake you in the summertime when the air conditioning in the sanctuary goes out. And the quilting, like I mentioned with those fabric squares at the center, and just going out and visiting folks down the road... I used to do all of that without a second thought. I was always on the move.

But now? Even with them calling and stopping by and trying to drag me out of the house, I just can't find that push inside me. Most days, I just sit at home in that recliner I told you about, and I leave the TV on real low, just a murmur, really, where you can barely even make out what the people on the screen are saying. I'll just sit there all afternoon, even though I know good and well that people are expecting me. I know they're looking at the clock at choir practice wondering where I am, or waiting on me to show up at the senior center, but the thought of getting up and going... it just isn't there anymore. 

So I don't think someone just encouraging me is going to fix it, doctor. Because they're already trying, bless their hearts, they really are. But no matter how much they encourage me or expect me to be somewhere, I just keep right on sitting there in the quiet.
Do you feel like you're in a low mood most of the time?

Low mood? Like... sad, you mean? Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't say I'm sad at all. It's funny you ask, though, because Mrs. Gable—I was just telling you about her, the one who dragged me to the senior center—she came over just the other evening carrying this big heavy blue Pyrex dish. It was one of those green bean casseroles, you know the kind with the little crispy fried onions sprinkled all over the top? My mother used to make them for Thanksgiving, though she always used fresh beans and I'm pretty sure Mrs. Gable uses canned, which just gets a bit mushy if you ask me. 

Anyway, she came bustling in through the screen door and set it right down on the coffee table, right on top of my TV Guide, and she started going on about how I must be feeling so blue, just sitting in this house all by my lonesome. I started grabbing those heavy metal chairs and dragging them all across the linoleum.
